claims.text: Very short high-temperature dwell times inhibit atomic mobility and are the key factor favoring a single-phase solid solution in rapidly synthesized noble-metal HEA nanoparticles.
Increasing the peak-temperature dwell time permits enough atomic motion to cause elemental segregation or alternate crystal structures.
A homogeneous, single-phase noble-metal HEA nanoparticle baseline can be produced through rapid heating and rapid cooling.
The baseline synthesis reaches approximately 2000 K for milliseconds.
The baseline cooling rate is approximately 10^4–10^5 K/s.
Dwell time can be varied while peak temperature, cooling rate, and composition are held constant.
The proposed mechanism is applicable to nanoparticles synthesized from at least five noble metals under rapid thermal cycling.
Increasing dwell time from milliseconds to seconds at approximately 2000 K increases atomic diffusion.
Effective atomic diffusion length or mobility is the structural mediator governing whether the nanoparticles remain uniformly mixed.
A brief thermal pulse limits diffusion and kinetically traps all elements in a uniform mixed state.
Extended high-temperature dwell enables diffusion that can cause segregation or crystal-structure changes.
Fast heating melts or fuses distinct precursors and mixes their constituent elements.
Rapid cooling freezes a high-entropy single-phase state.
Prolonged high-temperature dwell lets atoms overcome kinetic barriers and nucleate segregated or secondary phases.
Compared with the millisecond-dwell baseline, second-scale dwell will produce elemental segregation, secondary phases, or a change from single FCC to mixed FCC/BCC or another structure.
Very long dwell times may cause complete melting and agglomeration that eliminate nanoscale effects.
The dwell-time threshold for segregation depends on elemental combination, particle size, and thermal diffusivity.
The hypothesis is falsified if increasing dwell time causes no detectable phase separation, compositional segregation, or structural modification relative to the baseline.
